articles.title: The Last Directory: a local ghost story with a paper trail
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. The Last Directory turns a fictional file index into three short ghost-story scenes, using a small ope…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built The Last Directory turns a fictional file index into three short ghost-story scenes, using a small open-weight model running locally. Each scene has a source chip. Click it and the archive line that inspired the scene lights up beside the story. The starting image is a station that has closed for the night. Its last train has left. A red umbrella has no owner. An announcement is queued for platform nine, although the station has only eight platforms. Those four notes are original fiction. So are the filenames and the station. Nothing on your computer is searched or opened.
articles.author: ChillG

articles.title: Works on localhost, silent from the phone: Windows Firewall rules for a LAN app
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a Wind…
articles.body: Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a Windows PC: you speak on the phone and the text appears at the PC cursor over local Wi-Fi. The PC side is a small Node.js helper that listens for the phone on the LAN: a TCP port for the connection, a UDP port for a discovery probe, and mDNS. For a while, a version of the helper did not add any firewall rules on purpose. The reasoning was reasonable: the first time an exe binds a listening socket, Windows shows its "Windows Security Alert: allow access?" popup, the user clicks Allow, done, and no UAC prompt from us.

articles.body: 👻 GhostWriter AI: Bringing Stories to Life with Local Open-Source AI This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built For this week's Hacktoberfest challenge, I explored an idea that combines Halloween, storytelling, and open-source artificial intelligence: GhostWriter AI — a local AI-powered horror story generator. The idea is simple: what if you could create your own spooky stories without sending your prompts to an external AI service? GhostWriter AI is designed to generate personalized horror stories based on a user's imagination. You can choose a setting, describe a mysterious event, select a mood, and let a locally running AI model turn those ideas into a chilling story.

articles.title: acme.sh on a Server Where certbot Will Not Install
articles.excerpt: Four sites on one legacy box went dark. Not slow, not 500 - dark, as in the TLS handshake failed before a request existed. They had been down for five days before anyone noticed, because nothing was w…
articles.body: Four sites on one legacy box went dark. Not slow, not 500 - dark, as in the TLS handshake failed before a request existed. They had been down for five days before anyone noticed, because nothing was watching the one thing that mattered. The cause was mundane: certificate renewal lived inside a control panel, the panel's licence expired, and its daily renewal cron died with it. Seven more certificates on the same machine were scheduled to expire over the following three weeks. The distro was years past end of life, so certbot would not install cleanly and the vendor packages were long gone. This is the recipe that fixed it in under thirty minutes without touching a single vhost file, and the monitoring that makes sure it cannot happen quietly again.
articles.author: UDAWPK

articles.title: Best Privacy-First Email for Developers in 2026: Proton vs Infomaniak
articles.excerpt: Every side project ends up needing two different things from email, and most guides only talk about one of them. The first is a human mailbox: you@yourdomain.dev, read on a laptop and a phone, kept aw…
articles.body: Every side project ends up needing two different things from email, and most guides only talk about one of them. The first is a human mailbox : you@yourdomain.dev , read on a laptop and a phone, kept away from an advertising company. The second is an outbound SMTP endpoint : the thing your app authenticates against at three in the morning to send a password reset. These are not the same job, the same traffic pattern, or the same failure mode, and the moment you treat them as one you get a project whose signups silently stop working. This is a comparison of the two privacy-first providers that are genuinely worth running a domain on in 2026, with the prices as they are billed today, the DNS records you will actually paste, and an honest line about where each one stops.
articles.author: UDAWPK

articles.title: Running a Green CI Pipeline Isn't the Hard Part Anymore
articles.excerpt: Six months ago, your team adopted an AI coding assistant. Pull requests doubled. Generated code started landing in branches faster than reviewers could read it. The CI pipeline kept up for about three…
articles.body: Six months ago, your team adopted an AI coding assistant. Pull requests doubled. Generated code started landing in branches faster than reviewers could read it. The CI pipeline kept up for about three weeks. Now the queue backs up by mid-morning. Builds take 38 minutes. 4,000 tests run on every commit when 60 are relevant. The pipeline was designed for developers writing code. It is now processing code that machines write, at machine speed, with human-era validation. This is for platform engineers and engineering leads dealing with what happens when AI-generated code meets a CI pipeline that was never built for that volume. Green is the baseline. It is not the finish line. AI writes the code faster. CI still validates it the slow way. The bottleneck shifted.

articles.title: Swift Explained: Apple's Language for iPhone, Mac, and More
articles.excerpt: Introduction Swift is Apple's language for its platforms: iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Apple TV. Introduced in 2014 to replace the older Objective-C, it was designed to be safe, fast, and — unu…
articles.body: Introduction Swift is Apple's language for its platforms: iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Apple TV. Introduced in 2014 to replace the older Objective-C, it was designed to be safe, fast, and — unusually for a systems language — genuinely pleasant to read and write. Even if you never ship an app, Swift teaches one idea every developer should understand: optionals. Optionals: saying "this might be missing" Most bugs in app development come from one cause: code assuming a value exists when it does not. Swift makes that assumption impossible to hide. A value that might be missing is wrapped in an Optional, and you must unwrap it before use. var nickname : String ?

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden Explanation: Sometimes it’s night on the ground but day in the air. As the Earth rotates to eclipse the Sun, sunset rises up from the ground. Therefore, at sunset on the ground, sunlight still shines on clouds above. Under usual circumstances , a pretty sunset might be visible, but unusual noctilucent clouds float so high up they can be seen well after dark.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.
